body:
Whose Will Am I Really Doing?

Intention · Priorities · Guidance · The Journey Itself

I. The Question Underneath Everything

This week's parsha gives us an opportunity to look at ourselves honestly and ask a single question that recurs throughout: am I doing what Hashem wants of me, or am I doing what I want, hoping Hashem will be okay with it? That question plays out more than once in Matos-Masei, in very different settings, and each time it asks us to examine not just our actions but the motives underneath them.

II. After the War: Facing the Past Honestly

As Bnei Yisrael return victorious from battle, Moshe sees the commanding officers, and he is upset. Why? Because the officers had allowed the Midianite women to live, the same women who, under Bilam's advice, had seduced Bnei Yisrael into immorality and idolatry. That spiritual downfall brought a devastating plague and the death of thousands.

The officers had to confront something uncomfortable about themselves. Am I here right now because I want something Hashem allows, or because I want something He does not? Am I approaching this with the right intentions, or am I hoping Hashem will be fine with what I had already decided to do regardless? Moshe Rabbeinu, under Hashem's guidance, draws a clear moral line between those who had been involved in bringing down Bnei Yisrael and those who had not. Through that clarity, the nation could reflect honestly and say: I see it now. Maybe I did not go into this with the right mindset. But thank Hashem I have leaders who can help me recalibrate.

III. Reuven and Gad: The Subtle Danger of Misaligned Priorities

We see a similar pattern later, though in a very different setting. The tribes of Reuven and Gad, who had large flocks and herds, ask Moshe to let them settle on the eastern side of the Jordan, outside the borders of Eretz Yisrael, because the land there suits their livestock well. The proposal sounds reasonable on its face. But Moshe reacts with sharp concern. He sees a dangerous parallel to the episode of the meraglim, the spies who discouraged entering the land and undermined the entire national mission.

Moshe challenges them directly: are you making this request out of genuine spiritual alignment, or are you prioritizing your own comfort and livelihood over Hashem's plan? The two tribes respond by promising to join the national army, lead the charge in battle, and only afterward return to settle the land they had requested. But pay attention to their own language:

גְּדֵרֹת צֹאן נִבְנֶה לְמִקְנֵנוּ פֹּה וְעָרִים לְטַפֵּנוּ

"We will build sheepfolds for our livestock here, and cities for our children."

— Bamidbar 32:16

Moshe's reply is subtle but deeply meaningful. He flips the order entirely:

בְּנוּ לָכֶם עָרִים לְטַפְּכֶם וּגְדֵרֹת לְצֹנַאֲכֶם

"Build cities for your children, and sheepfolds for your livestock."

— Bamidbar 32:24

This is not a stylistic edit. It is a values correction. They spoke first of property, then of people. Moshe responds by restoring the correct priority: your families, your children, your future, must always come first. Livelihood matters, but it is not the foundation. Our homes, our Torah, our children, our values, these must be the center. Even when we think we are doing something spiritual, if it is not grounded in Hashem's will, if it is rooted instead in our own preferences or comfort, it loses its kedushah.

IV. The Role of Guidance

These two episodes, one harsh and one nuanced, share a common theme: the value of leadership and redirection. In both stories, Bnei Yisrael had Moshe Rabbeinu there to ask the hard questions, to challenge assumptions, and to help them realign their intentions with Hashem's will. Most of us are blessed with teachers, friends, rabbanim, and mentors, people who help us evaluate ourselves honestly. But their guidance only helps if we are actually willing to listen.

It is easy to say: I found a source that permits it, or, I am following my heart, I do not need to be told what to do. But Torah is not simply a checklist. It is a living structure, a path of refinement. It does not only ask what are you doing. It asks why are you doing it, how are you doing it, and whose values are actually guiding you, yours or Hashem's.

V. Masei: The Journey Itself Is the Message

As we move into Parshas Masei, the Torah begins listing the forty-two places Bnei Yisrael traveled during their years in the desert. At first glance, it looks like a dry travel log. But it carries real meaning. The Baal Shem Tov teaches that these forty-two journeys parallel the stages each of us moves through across a lifetime, from birth to death, from clarity to confusion and back again. Every stop, every phase, every challenge has something to teach.

It invites us to look honestly at our own life. Where have I been? Where am I now? Where am I going? We change. Our circumstances shift. But the question underneath all of it remains the same: am I navigating life on my own terms, or am I open to being guided by Hashem's terms?

VI. Doing the Right Thing for the Right Reason

Sometimes we start out with the wrong intention. Sometimes we fight the battles Hashem wants us to fight, but we want to keep the spoils for ourselves. Sometimes we want to sit and learn Torah, but really Hashem wants us to go out and build. That is exactly why we need leaders, rabbanim, friends, people who care enough to tell us the truth and help us check our motives, adjusting course when necessary.

So we return to the question one more time: am I doing what Hashem wants of me, or am I doing what I want and simply hoping He will go along with it? When we have the courage to ask that honestly, and the humility to accept guidance when it comes, we can walk our own journey with clarity, strength, and purpose. May we all be blessed to walk our own forty-two journeys with awareness, with faith, and with the willingness to be guided, so that in the end we can say we lived not only a life of Torah, but a life of true alignment with the ratzon Hashem.

חזק ואחזק

Good Shabbos

Reflection Questions

• Am I doing what Hashem wants of me, or am I doing what I want and hoping Hashem will be okay with it?

• Is there a decision I made recently where I should pause and ask honestly whether my mindset going in was actually aligned with Hashem's will?

• In my own life, am I putting property before people, or people before property? What would it look like to flip that order the way Moshe did for Reuven and Gad?

• Who in my life plays the role Moshe played for Bnei Yisrael, asking me the hard questions and helping me realign? Am I actually listening to them?

• Looking at my own forty-two journeys, where have I been, where am I now, and where am I going? What is this current stage trying to teach me?

• Where in my life am I navigating on my own terms rather than being open to Hashem's terms? What would it take to shift that?
